questions.q: Why is running N vectorized environment copies usually faster than running one at a time, even with the same total hardware?
options: It reduces the size of the neural network needed
A single environment leaves hardware mostly idle waiting on environment stepping, so batching N copies turns N sequential calls into one call and yields N transitions per step
Vectorization automatically reduces the discount factor
It eliminates the need for a reward function
questions.explain: Collecting experience is usually the bottleneck, not the gradient update. Batching N sub-environments together increases data-collection throughput.

questions.q: What does gym.make_vec("CartPole-v1", num_envs=8, vectorization_mode="sync") return?
options: 8 independent environments with no shared interface
A single environment with an 8x larger action space
A vectorized environment wrapper where reset() and step() operate on batches of 8 across a leading dimension
A pretrained policy for CartPole
questions.explain: make_vec wraps num_envs copies of the named environment, batching observations, rewards, and termination signals along a leading dimension.

questions.q: What is the key difference between SyncVectorEnv and AsyncVectorEnv?
options: SyncVectorEnv only supports Discrete action spaces
SyncVectorEnv steps sub-environments sequentially in one process; AsyncVectorEnv runs each sub-environment in its own subprocess for true parallelism
AsyncVectorEnv cannot be created with gym.make_vec
SyncVectorEnv requires a GPU
questions.explain: Sync vectorization steps environments one after another in-process (low overhead, good for cheap environments); async vectorization uses subprocesses, which pays off when each environment step is itself expensive.

questions.q: What is autoreset in the context of vectorized environments?
options: The vectorized wrapper automatically resetting a sub-environment that just finished, typically reflected on the next step() call
A setting that disables the terminated flag
A feature that restarts training if loss diverges
The default seed used when none is provided
questions.explain: Because sub-environments finish at different times, the vectorized wrapper automatically resets a finished one, which means a later observation batch can mix a fresh episode's first observation with another sub-environment's mid-episode observation.

questions.q: Why should training code check terminations/truncations per index rather than assuming every row in a vectorized batch is mid-episode?
options: Because indices are randomly shuffled every step
Because autoreset means some sub-environments may have just started a new episode while others are mid-episode, so return bookkeeping must be tracked per sub-environment
Because the action_space differs per index
Because rewards are shared across all sub-environments
questions.explain: Sub-environments finish and autoreset independently, so correctly crediting returns to the right episode requires per-index tracking of terminations and truncations.
